questions.questionText: You want to retain control over the encryption keys used to protect your Cloud Storage data, but you want Google to manage the hardware, key lifecycle, and high availability. Which encryption option should you choose?
correctAnswers: Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK)

explanation.general explanation: Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) allow you to generate and manage your own encryption keys within Google Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS) while Google handles the underlying hardware, durability, and high availability.

why other options are wrong.Google-default encryption: With Google-default encryption, Google manages the keys completely, so you do not have direct control over the key lifecycle or rotation.
why other options are wrong.Customer-Supplied Encryption Keys (CSEK): CSEK requires you to manage the key material yourself and supply it with every API call, which means Google is not managing the key lifecycle.
why other options are wrong.Cloud External Key Manager (Cloud EKM): Cloud EKM is used when you want to manage keys outside of Google Cloud in a third-party key manager, not when you want Google to manage the hardware and lifecycle.

questions.questionText: Your compliance team requires that the encryption keys used for BigQuery datasets must be generated and protected by a hardware device certified to FIPS 140-2 Level 3. Which Cloud KMS feature provides this?
correctAnswers: Cloud HSM

explanation.general explanation: Cloud HSM (Hardware Security Module) is a cloud-hosted key management service that allows you to protect encryption keys within a FIPS 140-2 Level 3 certified hardware device managed by Google.

why other options are wrong.Cloud EKM: Cloud EKM connects to an external key manager. While that external manager might be an HSM, Cloud EKM itself is just the bridge, whereas Cloud HSM is Google's native FIPS 140-2 Level 3 offering.
why other options are wrong.Software-backed CMEK: Standard software-backed CMEK keys are protected by Google's infrastructure (which meets FIPS 140-2 Level 1) but not by dedicated Level 3 hardware modules.
why other options are wrong.Customer-Supplied Encryption Keys (CSEK): CSEK requires you to provide the key material; it does not utilize Google's Cloud HSM.

questions.questionText: Your company's security policy states that all encryption keys must reside entirely within your on-premises data center, and Google Cloud must never have access to the raw key material. However, you still want to use these keys to encrypt BigQuery data. Which service allows this?
correctAnswers: Cloud EKM (External Key Manager)

explanation.general explanation: Cloud External Key Manager (Cloud EKM) lets you encrypt data in Google Cloud using keys that are stored and managed in a supported third-party key management system residing outside Google's infrastructure.

why other options are wrong.Cloud HSM: Cloud HSM keys are managed and stored within Google's data centers, which violates the requirement to keep keys strictly on-premises.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Storage CSEK: CSEK requires sending the raw key material to Google's memory for encryption operations, violating the policy that Google must never have access to the raw key material.
why other options are wrong.Standard Cloud KMS: Standard CMEK keys are generated and stored within Google Cloud.

questions.questionText: In Google Cloud, what is the fundamental architecture used to encrypt user data when using Cloud KMS?
correctAnswers: Envelope encryption

explanation.general explanation: Google Cloud uses Envelope Encryption. Data is encrypted locally using a Data Encryption Key (DEK). The DEK itself is then encrypted using a Key Encryption Key (KEK), which is securely stored and managed in Cloud KMS.

why other options are wrong.Symmetric stream ciphering: While symmetric ciphers are used, the overarching architectural pattern for managing the keys is envelope encryption.
why other options are wrong.Asymmetric public key exchange: This is a method for securely exchanging keys over a network, not the storage pattern used by Cloud KMS for data at rest.
why other options are wrong.Hash-based message authentication: HMACs are used for verifying data integrity and authenticity, not for encrypting large volumes of data at rest.

questions.questionText: You are creating a Key Ring in Cloud KMS. Which of the following statements is true regarding Key Rings?
options: The location of a Key Ring cannot be changed and it cannot be deleted.
A Key Ring can be moved to a different region at any time.
Key Rings are automatically deleted if they contain no keys.
You can change the name of a Key Ring after it is created.
correctAnswers: The location of a Key Ring cannot be changed and it cannot be deleted.

explanation.general explanation: In Cloud KMS, Key Rings are organizational resources used to group keys. Once a Key Ring is created, its name and location are immutable. Furthermore, Key Rings and Keys cannot be deleted to ensure an audit trail and prevent accidental permanent data loss.

why other options are wrong.A Key Ring can be moved to a different r: The location of a Key Ring is immutable upon creation.
why other options are wrong.Key Rings are automatically deleted if t: Key Rings cannot be deleted, automatically or manually.
why other options are wrong.You can change the name of a Key Ring af: The name of a Key Ring is permanent and cannot be changed.

questions.questionText: You need to grant a service account the ability to encrypt and decrypt data using a specific CMEK key, but you do not want to give it permission to destroy or rotate the key. Which IAM role should you assign?
correctAnswers: roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter

explanation.general explanation: The 'roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter' role grants exactly the permissions needed to use a key for encryption and decryption, without granting administrative privileges to modify, rotate, or destroy the key.

why other options are wrong.roles/cloudkms.admin: The Admin role allows users to manage the key's lifecycle (create, destroy, rotate), which violates the requirement.
why other options are wrong.roles/owner: The Owner role provides full administrative access to the entire project.
why other options are wrong.roles/cloudkms.viewer: The Viewer role only provides read access to see the key's metadata; it does not allow the user to perform encryption or decryption operations.

questions.questionText: You want to securely and permanently remove an encryption key from Cloud KMS so the associated data becomes permanently unreadable. What is the standard process for doing this?
options: Schedule the key version for destruction.
Click the 'Delete Key' button in the Cloud Console.
Run a command to immediately overwrite the key material.
Delete the Google Cloud Project containing the key.
correctAnswers: Schedule the key version for destruction.

explanation.general explanation: Because deleting a key leads to permanent data loss, Cloud KMS does not have a simple 'Delete' button. Instead, you must schedule the key version for destruction, which initiates a grace period (default 24 hours) before the key material is permanently destroyed.

why other options are wrong.Click the 'Delete Key' button in the Clo: There is no 'Delete Key' button. Keys cannot be directly deleted; they must be scheduled for destruction.
why other options are wrong.Run a command to immediately overwrite t: Cloud KMS does not allow users to execute commands to immediately overwrite underlying hardware key material.
why other options are wrong.Delete the Google Cloud Project containi: While deleting a project will eventually purge its resources, it is a destructive action affecting the entire project, not the standard process for destroying a single KMS key.

questions.questionText: To comply with internal security policies, all symmetric encryption keys must be rotated automatically every 90 days. Does Cloud KMS support this feature natively?
options: Yes, Cloud KMS supports automatic rotation for symmetric keys.
No, all key rotations in Cloud KMS must be done manually.
Yes, but only for asymmetric keys.
No, Cloud KMS relies on Cloud Functions for key rotation.
correctAnswers: Yes, Cloud KMS supports automatic rotation for symmetric keys.

explanation.general explanation: Cloud KMS natively supports automatic key rotation for symmetric keys. You can specify a rotation period (e.g., 90 days), and Cloud KMS will automatically generate a new primary key version at that interval.

why other options are wrong.No, all key rotations in Cloud KMS must: Cloud KMS supports both manual and automatic rotation.
Automatic rotation is supported for symmetric keys, not asymmetric keys. Asymmetric keys must be rotated manually.
why other options are wrong.No, Cloud KMS relies on Cloud Functions: While you can script rotation, Cloud KMS provides automatic rotation as a native, built-in feature.

questions.questionText: You are using Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) to encrypt a Cloud Storage bucket. Which identity actually makes the API calls to Cloud KMS to encrypt and decrypt the objects?
options: A custom Compute Engine Service Account.
correctAnswers: The Cloud Storage Service Agent.

explanation.general explanation: When using CMEK with a Google Cloud service like Cloud Storage, the service itself performs the encryption on your behalf. Therefore, the Cloud Storage Service Agent (a Google-managed service account specific to your project) must be granted the Encrypter/Decrypter role to make the calls to KMS.

The end-user does not directly encrypt the data; they upload plaintext, and Cloud Storage encrypts it seamlessly in the background.
The encryption operations for the bucket are handled by the Cloud Storage backend service agent, not a user-created Compute Engine VM account.
The Project Owner is a human role; automated background encryption is performed by the service agent.

questions.questionText: To enforce Separation of Duties, which IAM role should you assign to the Security team so they can manage the KMS key lifecycle (create, rotate, destroy) without being able to encrypt or decrypt actual application data?
correctAnswers: roles/cloudkms.admin

explanation.general explanation: The 'roles/cloudkms.admin' role allows an administrator to create key rings, create keys, and manage key rotation and destruction. It explicitly excludes the ability to use the keys for encryption or decryption, supporting strict Separation of Duties.

why other options are wrong.roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypt: This role grants data access (encryption/decryption), which the security team should not have.
why other options are wrong.roles/editor: The primitive Editor role grants broad permissions across the project, violating least privilege.
why other options are wrong.roles/cloudkms.viewer: The Viewer role is read-only and does not allow the security team to create or rotate keys.

questions.questionText: You are designing an architecture for a large enterprise. Where is the best place to host Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) to ensure strict separation of duties between security administrators and application developers?
options: In a dedicated, centralized Google Cloud Project solely for KMS.
In the same project as the application, but using different tags.
In the default Compute Engine project.
correctAnswers: In a dedicated, centralized Google Cloud Project solely for KMS.

explanation.general explanation: Creating a dedicated, centralized KMS project is the best practice for large enterprises. It allows you to grant the Security Team admin rights on the KMS project, while Application Developers only have rights in their application projects, ensuring strict Separation of Duties at the project boundary.

why other options are wrong.In the same project as the application,: Placing keys in the same project means Project Owners/Editors have access to both the application and the keys, which weakens separation of duties. Tags are for networking/billing, not IAM isolation.
KMS keys are managed in the cloud, not on local laptops.
Using a shared or default compute project mixes application resources with security keys, failing to provide boundary isolation.

questions.questionText: You have encrypted a Compute Engine Persistent Disk with a CMEK. What happens to a running VM if you disable the active KMS key version used by that disk?
options: The VM will continue running, but subsequent start/restart operations will fail.
The VM will immediately shut down.
The VM will automatically switch to Google-default encryption.
The VM's data will be instantly deleted.
correctAnswers: The VM will continue running, but subsequent start/restart operations will fail.

explanation.general explanation: Compute Engine utilizes the CMEK key to decrypt the Data Encryption Key (DEK) into memory when the VM starts. If you disable the KMS key while the VM is running, the running VM is unaffected because the DEK is already in memory. However, if the VM is stopped or restarted, it will fail to boot because it can no longer decrypt the DEK.

Disabling a key does not forcefully evict the already decrypted DEK from the VM's active RAM.
why other options are wrong.The VM will automatically switch to Goog: Encryption configurations are static; it will not automatically re-encrypt data with a different key.
Disabling a key makes the data inaccessible on next boot, but it does not delete the ciphertext data from the disk.

questions.questionText: You need to directly encrypt a small 10 KB configuration file using the Cloud KMS API without writing your own envelope encryption logic. Is this supported by Cloud KMS?
options: Yes, Cloud KMS supports direct encryption of plaintext payloads up to 64 KB.
No, Cloud KMS only encrypts Data Encryption Keys (DEKs).
Yes, Cloud KMS can directly encrypt files of any size.
No, you must always use Cloud Storage to encrypt files.
correctAnswers: Yes, Cloud KMS supports direct encryption of plaintext payloads up to 64 KB.

explanation.general explanation: While Cloud KMS is designed primarily for envelope encryption (encrypting DEKs), the Cloud KMS API does support direct encryption and decryption of small amounts of plaintext data, up to a maximum size of 64 KB.

why other options are wrong.No, Cloud KMS only encrypts Data Encrypt: This is false; it can encrypt any small payload directly.
why other options are wrong.Yes, Cloud KMS can directly encrypt file: Direct KMS encryption has a strict limit of 64 KB to prevent performance bottlenecks. Larger files require envelope encryption.
why other options are wrong.No, you must always use Cloud Storage to: You can use the KMS API directly from any application without storing the file in Cloud Storage.

questions.questionText: Can you recover a Cloud KMS key version after the scheduled destruction period has passed and it is fully destroyed?
options: No, once a key version is destroyed, the key material cannot be recovered.
Yes, you can contact Google Support within 30 days.
Yes, the key material is archived in Cloud Storage.
Yes, but only if you have the Cloud KMS Admin role.
correctAnswers: No, once a key version is destroyed, the key material cannot be recovered.

explanation.general explanation: Cloud KMS guarantees cryptographic erasure. Once a key version's scheduled destruction period expires and it is fully destroyed, the underlying cryptographic key material is permanently deleted and cannot be recovered by anyone, including Google Support.

why other options are wrong.Yes, you can contact Google Support with: Google Support cannot recover destroyed key material.
why other options are wrong.Yes, the key material is archived in Clo: Key material is never exported or archived to Cloud Storage.
why other options are wrong.Yes, but only if you have the Cloud KMS: Even KMS Admins cannot recover a fully destroyed key.

questions.questionText: You want to use CMEK with a Cloud SQL database. At what stage of the database lifecycle must you specify the KMS key?
options: When creating the Cloud SQL instance.
When running the first SQL INSERT statement.
After the instance is created, by modifying its settings.
correctAnswers: When creating the Cloud SQL instance.

explanation.general explanation: For services like Cloud SQL, the encryption configuration is set at the infrastructure level. You must specify the CMEK key during the initial creation of the Cloud SQL instance. You cannot apply CMEK to an existing instance that was created with default encryption.

why other options are wrong.When running the first SQL INSERT statem: Encryption is configured at the storage volume level, not at the query execution level.
why other options are wrong.After the instance is created, by modify: You cannot alter the encryption type of a Cloud SQL instance after it has been created.
Backups inherit the encryption of the primary instance, which must be configured at creation.

questions.questionText: A security administrator accidentally scheduled a critical KMS key for destruction. By default, how long is the grace period before the destruction becomes permanent and the data becomes unrecoverable?
correctAnswers: 24 hours

explanation.general explanation: By default, when you schedule a Cloud KMS key version for destruction, a 24-hour grace period begins. During this 24-hour window, an administrator can cancel the destruction to save the key. (Note: The duration can be customized, but the default is 24 hours).

why other options are wrong.1 hour: 1 hour is too short for a default safety buffer.
why other options are wrong.7 days: While you can configure custom destruction schedules, the default is 24 hours.
why other options are wrong.30 days: While you can configure custom destruction schedules up to 120 days, the default is 24 hours.

questions.questionText: You are using Cloud KMS for asymmetric cryptography to generate digital signatures. Which TWO types of asymmetric keys are supported by Cloud KMS? (Select two)
correctAnswers: RSA keys
Elliptic Curve (EC) keys

explanation.general explanation: Cloud KMS supports asymmetric keys for both digital signatures and asymmetric encryption. The two mathematical algorithms supported for asymmetric keys in Cloud KMS are RSA and Elliptic Curve (EC).

why other options are wrong.Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) keys: AES is a symmetric encryption algorithm, not asymmetric.
why other options are wrong.Blowfish keys: Blowfish is an older symmetric cipher not used by Cloud KMS.
why other options are wrong.DES keys: DES is an outdated symmetric cipher.

questions.questionText: Mountkirk Games (Case Study) wants to encrypt global player data using CMEK. The data is stored in a multi-region Cloud Storage bucket. To ensure the integration works, what must be true about the KMS Key Ring location?
options: The Key Ring must be created in the same multi-region location as the Cloud Storage bucket.
The Key Ring must be 'global' regardless of the bucket location.
The Key Ring must be located in a single region.
The Key Ring location does not matter.
correctAnswers: The Key Ring must be created in the same multi-region location as the Cloud Storage bucket.

explanation.general explanation: When using CMEK with Google Cloud services like Cloud Storage or BigQuery, the location of the KMS Key Ring must match the location of the resource it is encrypting. If the bucket is in a multi-region (e.g., 'us'), the Key Ring must also be created in the 'us' multi-region.

why other options are wrong.The Key Ring must be 'global' regardless: While global keys exist, Cloud Storage explicitly requires the KMS key location to match the bucket location.
why other options are wrong.The Key Ring must be located in a single: If the bucket is multi-region, the key cannot be in a single region; they must match exactly.
Location strictly matters for CMEK integrations.

questions.questionText: Your company detects a severe security breach and wants to immediately prevent all access to a Cloud Storage bucket encrypted with CMEK. What is the fastest and most reliable way to revoke decryption access?
options: Disable the active KMS key version.
Enable Object Versioning on the bucket.
Remove the storage.objectViewer role from all users.
correctAnswers: Disable the active KMS key version.

explanation.general explanation: Disabling the active KMS key version provides a cryptographic access kill switch. Once the key is disabled, Cloud Storage immediately fails to decrypt any data, rendering the entire bucket unreadable without having to track down and modify IAM policies across hundreds of users.

Rotating a key creates a new version for future encryption, but the old version remains active to decrypt existing data, so access is not blocked.
Object Versioning protects against accidental deletion; it does not block data access.
why other options are wrong.Remove the storage.objectViewer role fro: Updating IAM policies can take time to propagate and is error-prone during a panic, whereas disabling the key is immediate and foolproof.

questions.questionText: What happens when you use Customer-Supplied Encryption Keys (CSEK) instead of Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK)?
options: You must provide the raw encryption key material with every API request.
Google stores your encryption key securely in Cloud KMS.
You can use Cloud IAM to manage access to the key.
The key is automatically rotated every 90 days by Google.
correctAnswers: You must provide the raw encryption key material with every API request.

explanation.general explanation: With Customer-Supplied Encryption Keys (CSEK), Google does not store your keys. You manage your keys entirely on your own systems and must supply the raw key material in the headers of every single API request you make to read or write data.

why other options are wrong.You can use Cloud IAM to manage access t: Since Google does not store the key in KMS, you cannot use IAM to manage access to it.
why other options are wrong.The key is automatically rotated every 9: Google has no access to the key material permanently, so it cannot rotate it.

questions.questionText: Which TWO of the following Google Cloud services natively support encrypting data at rest using Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK)? (Select two)
correctAnswers: Cloud Storage
BigQuery

explanation.general explanation: CMEK is heavily integrated into Google Cloud's core storage and analytics products. Both Cloud Storage and BigQuery offer native, seamless integration with Cloud KMS to encrypt data at rest using customer-managed keys.

why other options are wrong.Google Workspace: Google Workspace (Docs, Gmail) uses its own client-side encryption mechanisms and does not natively integrate with GCP Cloud KMS in the same way infrastructure services do.
why other options are wrong.App Engine Memcache: Memcache is an in-memory, volatile service and does not support CMEK for data at rest.
why other options are wrong.Memorystore for Redis: While Memorystore encrypts data using Google-managed keys, as of standard configurations, it does not support CMEK for its volatile memory stores.

questions.questionText: What are TWO primary differences between Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) and Customer-Supplied Encryption Keys (CSEK)? (Select two)
options: CMEK keys are stored and managed within Google Cloud KMS, whereas CSEK keys are not stored by Google.
CSEK requires you to send the raw key material with your API calls, whereas CMEK relies on IAM permissions for key access.
CMEK is only supported for asymmetric encryption.
CSEK automatically rotates keys every 30 days.
CMEK requires an on-premises hardware security module.
correctAnswers: CMEK keys are stored and managed within Google Cloud KMS, whereas CSEK keys are not stored by Google.
CSEK requires you to send the raw key material with your API calls, whereas CMEK relies on IAM permissions for key access.

explanation.general explanation: The defining differences are storage and delivery. CMEK keys are securely stored inside Google Cloud KMS, allowing applications to use them via IAM permissions. CSEK keys are kept strictly by the customer, meaning Google never stores them, and the customer must actively transmit the raw key with every read/write API call.

why other options are wrong.CMEK is only supported for asymmetric en: CMEK primarily uses symmetric encryption for envelope data encryption.
why other options are wrong.CSEK automatically rotates keys every 30: CSEK keys cannot be rotated by Google because Google does not hold them.
why other options are wrong.CMEK requires an on-premises hardware se: CMEK is fully cloud-native. Cloud EKM is the service that connects to on-premises hardware.

questions.questionText: Which TWO IAM roles are critical for implementing Separation of Duties for Cloud KMS administrators and application services? (Select two)
correctAnswers: roles/cloudkms.admin
roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter

explanation.general explanation: To ensure Separation of Duties, security administrators are granted 'roles/cloudkms.admin' to manage the keys without being able to see the data. Service agents and applications are granted 'roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter' to use the keys without being able to modify or delete them.

why other options are wrong.roles/storage.admin: This manages Cloud Storage, not Cloud KMS separation of duties.
why other options are wrong.roles/iam.serviceAccountUser: This allows a user to act as a service account, but does not dictate KMS encryption permissions.

questions.questionText: You are configuring a Cloud Storage bucket in Project A to use a CMEK key stored in Project B. Which TWO steps are required to establish this cross-project encryption? (Select two)
options: Grant the Cloud Storage Service Agent of Project A the 'Encrypter/Decrypter' role on the KMS key in Project B.
Specify the KMS key resource ID when creating the Cloud Storage bucket in Project A.
Export the KMS key from Project B and import it into Project A.
Configure a VPC Network Peering connection between Project A and Project B.
Assign the 'Owner' role to all users in Project A.
correctAnswers: Grant the Cloud Storage Service Agent of Project A the 'Encrypter/Decrypter' role on the KMS key in Project B.
Specify the KMS key resource ID when creating the Cloud Storage bucket in Project A.

explanation.general explanation: Cross-project CMEK is a standard best practice. To make it work, you must authorize the service agent from the resource project (Project A) to use the key in the central KMS project (Project B) using IAM. Then, you simply configure the bucket in Project A to point to that specific key's URI.

why other options are wrong.Export the KMS key from Project B and im: Cloud KMS keys cannot be exported. They must remain in KMS.
why other options are wrong.Configure a VPC Network Peering connecti: KMS API calls are made over Google's internal backbone; they do not require VPC peering.
why other options are wrong.Assign the 'Owner' role to all users in: This violates the principle of least privilege and is completely unnecessary.

questions.questionText: What TWO benefits does Cloud HSM provide over standard software-backed Cloud KMS keys? (Select two)
options: Hardware keys are FIPS 140-2 Level 3 certified.
The key material never leaves the secure hardware boundary.
Hardware keys are free of charge.
Cloud HSM automatically copies keys to on-premises servers.
correctAnswers: Hardware keys are FIPS 140-2 Level 3 certified.
The key material never leaves the secure hardware boundary.

explanation.general explanation: Cloud HSM utilizes physical Hardware Security Modules. This provides two massive compliance benefits: the physical hardware is certified to the stringent FIPS 140-2 Level 3 standard, and the cryptographic operations happen entirely inside the hardware chip, meaning the raw key material never leaves the secure boundary.

Cloud HSM keys incur premium pricing compared to standard software keys.
why other options are wrong.Cloud HSM automatically copies keys to o: Cloud HSM keys cannot be exported to on-premises servers.
CSEK is customer-supplied; Cloud HSM generates and protects keys managed by Google.

questions.questionText: Which TWO key management options allow you to maintain control over your own encryption keys while still leveraging Google's managed services for data processing? (Select two)
correctAnswers: Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK)
Cloud External Key Manager (Cloud EKM)

explanation.general explanation: Both CMEK and Cloud EKM integrate directly with Google Cloud services (like BigQuery and Cloud Storage), allowing you to maintain control over the key lifecycle (creating, rotating, and destroying keys) while Google handles the heavy lifting of the data processing and storage.

why other options are wrong.Google-default encryption: Google controls the keys completely, so you do not maintain control over the key lifecycle.
why other options are wrong.Plaintext storage: Storing data in plaintext provides zero encryption or key control.
why other options are wrong.AWS KMS: While a valid service, it does not natively integrate with GCP services for at-rest envelope encryption like Cloud EKM or CMEK does.

questions.questionText: What TWO actions can you take on a specific Cloud KMS key version to temporarily prevent it from being used to decrypt data, without permanently destroying the key material? (Select two)
options: Remove the IAM 'Encrypter/Decrypter' bindings from the users or service agents.
correctAnswers: Disable the key version.
Remove the IAM 'Encrypter/Decrypter' bindings from the users or service agents.

explanation.general explanation: To temporarily block access, you can simply toggle the state of the key version to 'Disabled', which immediately halts all encryption/decryption operations. Alternatively, you can remove the IAM permissions that allow service agents to use the key. Both actions are fully reversible.

This initiates the permanent destruction process, which is not intended for temporary suspension.
Key locations are permanent and cannot be changed.

questions.questionText: You are designing an architecture and need to decide between Symmetric and Asymmetric encryption in Cloud KMS. For encrypting large volumes of data (like BigQuery datasets or Cloud Storage buckets) using CMEK, which key type is required?
correctAnswers: Symmetric encryption keys

explanation.general explanation: When integrating CMEK with Google Cloud storage and analytics services, the underlying envelope encryption architecture relies exclusively on Symmetric encryption keys. The same symmetric KEK is used to both encrypt and decrypt the underlying Data Encryption Keys (DEKs).

why other options are wrong.Asymmetric RSA keys: Asymmetric keys are used for digital signatures or asymmetric encryption of small payloads, but are not supported as the CMEK type for bulk data services like Cloud Storage.
why other options are wrong.Asymmetric Elliptic Curve keys: EC keys are used for digital signatures, not for CMEK envelope encryption.
why other options are wrong.Hash-based signatures: Hashing is for integrity, not for data encryption.

questions.questionText: You want to audit all decryption events for your CMEK keys to ensure that no unauthorized users are accessing sensitive data. What feature must you enable in Google Cloud?
options: Data Access audit logs for the Cloud KMS API
Admin Activity audit logs for Cloud KMS
correctAnswers: Data Access audit logs for the Cloud KMS API

explanation.general explanation: To see exactly when a key is used to encrypt or decrypt data, you must explicitly enable Data Access audit logs for the Cloud KMS API. These logs track 'who accessed what data' and are disabled by default due to high volume.

why other options are wrong.Admin Activity audit logs for Cloud KMS: Admin Activity logs (enabled by default) show when keys are created or deleted, but they do NOT show routine data encryption/decryption events.
why other options are wrong.VPC Flow Logs: VPC Flow Logs track network packet metadata, not Cloud KMS API invocations.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Storage access logs: These log bucket access, but if you want to audit the explicit decryption usage of the cryptographic key, you must look at the KMS API logs.

questions.questionText: A junior developer asks how data is encrypted in Google Cloud if no CMEK or CSEK is explicitly configured. What is the correct response?
options: By default, Google Cloud automatically encrypts all customer content at rest using Google-managed encryption keys.
By default, data is stored in plaintext unless CMEK is configured.
By default, data is only encrypted if it is placed in a 'Secure' storage class.
By default, data is encrypted using an open-source AES key shared across the project.
correctAnswers: By default, Google Cloud automatically encrypts all customer content at rest using Google-managed encryption keys.

explanation.general explanation: Google Cloud has a strict 'secure by default' posture. If a customer does not configure CMEK or CSEK, Google Cloud still automatically encrypts 100% of customer content at rest using AES-256 keys that are generated and managed by Google.

why other options are wrong.By default, data is stored in plaintext: This is false; Google Cloud never stores customer content in plaintext at rest.
why other options are wrong.By default, data is only encrypted if it: All storage classes are encrypted by default.
why other options are wrong.By default, data is encrypted using an o: Google uses distinct, granular Data Encryption Keys (DEKs) for different chunks of data, not a single shared key.
